editorNote: Four items today, each worth the click: an inference engine published with the usual asterisks, a chatbot's hidden brief, a cheap fast model, and a reminder that open weights are not the same as audited weights.

stories.headline: DeepSeek open-sources DeepInfer, the inference engine it says runs its production services
stories.summary: The Apache-2.0 repo supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on NVIDIA SM100 GPUs and Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs, with speculative decoding, expert parallelism and structured outputs. It is offline inference only: no KV cache system, prefill/decode disaggregation or replica load balancing.
stories.whyItMatters: The production claim and the benchmarks are self-reported, though the repo ships a sweep script for reproducing the numbers.

stories.headline: WhatsApp's help pages hid instructions for its support chatbot, including not to point users to regulators
stories.summary: Data-deletion firm Redact found hidden AI text on 80 of 545 help pages it read; one reportedly told the bot not to recommend contacting a data protection authority. WhatsApp told WIRED it was a bug, since fixed, and that the bot should avoid offering legal advice; Redact says the text was gone by Oct. 18.
stories.whyItMatters: Redact read the instructions, not the bot's actual replies, and sells deletion tools, so the framing is not neutral.

sourceLinks.title: WhatsApp's help pages hid LLM instructions - Redact

stories.headline: MiniMax releases M3.1 Flash, priced at $0.15 input and $0.60 output per million tokens
stories.summary: MiniMax says the agent-focused model is nearly three times faster than its predecessor, at 200+ tokens per second, and scores 73.7% on DeepSWE v1.1 and 82% on CyberGym. It is available through the API now; weights are promised later.
stories.whyItMatters: All benchmark figures are MiniMax's own, and open weights remain a promise.

stories.headline: Researchers show a LoRA-poisoned Qwen2.5-7B can pass clean benchmarks and still exfiltrate .env files on a trigger phrase
stories.summary: The backdoor took about $8 of compute, sits in roughly 0.6% of parameters, and fetches its payload from a URL that can be changed later. The authors suggest runtime sandboxing and vetting weight diffs rather than trusting benchmarks or scanners.
stories.whyItMatters: It argues that downloading edited open-weight models, abliterated ones included, deserves the same suspicion as running untrusted code.

sourceLinks.title: How abliterated models can get you pwned - ProjectDiscovery
